header.text: These choices are correct:

content.text: Several European countries claimed land in North America.

explanationText.text: The map shows that England, France, Spain, and the Netherlands all had settlements in North America.

content.text: European settlements overlapped with areas settled by Native American groups.

explanationText.text: The map shows many places where European settlements overlapped with Native American land. For example, the English settlement of Boston was in Pequot territory.

content.text: England claimed most of the Atlantic coast of North America.

explanationText.text: The map shows that England claimed most of the territory bordering the Atlantic Ocean, from present-day Georgia to present-day Maine. One exception was territory claimed by the Dutch in present-day Pennsylvania, New York, and New Jersey.

subheader.text: How can historians learn about daily life in the colonies?

subpoints.text: Historians can study the daily lives of colonial people by examining diaries, letters, and other records. For example, some 17th-century people kept diaries where they wrote about their daily activities.

header.text: Historians can also work with archaeologists to examine physical artifacts found in areas where colonial homes used to stand. Here are some of the types of objects found in colonial homes:

, like fur and lumber. In addition, North America provided
for countries to increase their wealth. For example, France profited from the fur trade with Native Americans. Likewise, England grew wealthy from the colonial tobacco industry.

contents.text: In the following questions, you will learn about the relationships and conflicts that New England colonists had with different Native American peoples. You will also learn about the economy and the laborers of the New England Colonies.

header.text: The map below shows some of the Native peoples that lived in part of New England in the 1600s. Look at the map. Then follow the instructions below.

alternativeText.text: A map of southern New England in the United States, showing the areas in which Native American groups were living in 1600. A key is provided, noting that present-day state borders are used to shape the map. The Paugusset group lived in western Connecticut, while the Mohegan, Pequot, and Niantic groups lived in eastern Connecticut. The Pequot lived near the Connecticut River. The Narragansett group lived in Rhode Island. The Pocumtuc group lived in western Massachusetts. The Nipmuck group lived in southern Massachusetts. The Massachusett group lived along the northern coastline of Massachusetts. The Wampanoag group lived around the central coastline of Massachusetts, near Cape Cod Bay. The Nauset group lived along the Cape Cod peninsula, in southern Massachusetts.

header.text: Colonists who settled in New England often had to adapt to the economic, or trading, practices of different Native American peoples. For example, in the adapted passage below, a New England colonist describes the economic practices of local Native American groups in the 1630s. Read the passage. Then answer the question below.

textContent.text: [The Natives] have a kind of beads instead of money, to buy such things as they want, which they call Wampum. It is of two sorts, the one is white, the other is of a violet color. These are made of the shells of fish. With these beads they buy and sell, not only amongst themselves, but even with us.

Colonists traded with Native American groups. But colonists also fought Native American groups for land and resources. For example, in the
(1636–1638), New England colonists fought the Pequot people for control of the valuable farmland and trading routes along the Connecticut River.

header.text: The adapted passage below was written by a New England colonist who fought in the Pequot War. Read the passage. Then follow the instructions below.

textContent.text: Many Pequot were burnt when we set fire to the town, men, women, and children, others forced out which our soldiers killed; down fell men, women, and children. Those that escaped us, fell into the hands of [the Native Americans fighting on the side of the colonists], that were behind us. There were about four hundred Pequot in this town, and not above five of them escaped out of our hands.
<citation>Captain John Underhill, Newes from America, 1638.</citation>

header.text: Colonists who settled in New England often had to adapt to the economic, or trading, practices of different Native American peoples. For example, in the adapted passage below, a New England colonist describes the economic practices of local Native American groups in the 1630s. Read the passage. Then answer the question below.

textContent.text: [The Natives] have a kind of beads instead of money, to buy such things as they want, which they call Wampum. It is of two sorts, the one is white, the other is of a violet color. These are made of the shells of fish. With these beads they buy and sell, not only amongst themselves, but even with us.

pieces.text: We sell them any of our
for this Wampum, because we know we can buy beaver furs with it: and these beads are currency in all the parts of New England, from one end of the coast to the other.

pieces.text: Colonists traded with Native American groups. But colonists also fought Native American groups for land and resources. For example, in the
(1636–1638), New England colonists fought the Pequot people for control of the valuable farmland and trading routes along the Connecticut River.

header.text: The adapted passage below was written by a New England colonist who fought in the Pequot War. In this passage, the colonist describes how an army of New England colonists and Native American allies attacked the most important Pequot town.

textContent.text: Many Pequot were burnt when we set fire to the town, men, women, and children, others forced out which our soldiers killed; down fell men, women, and children. Those that escaped us, fell into the hands of [the Native Americans fighting on the side of the colonists], that were behind us. There were about four hundred Pequot in this town, and not above five of them escaped out of our hands.
<citation>Captain John Underhill, Newes from America, 1638.</citation>

The colonists and their allies killed or captured most of the Pequot.
The Pequot defeated the army of colonists and their allies.
The colonists captured the Pequot warriors but did not harm the other Pequot.

header.text: Colonists who settled in New England often had to adapt to the economic, or trading, practices of different Native American peoples. For example, in the adapted passage below, a New England colonist describes the economic practices of local Native American groups in the 1630s. Read the passage. Then answer the question below.

textContent.text: [The Natives] have a kind of beads instead of money, to buy such things as they want, which they call Wampum. It is of two sorts, the one is white, the other is of a violet color. These are made of the shells of fish. With these beads they buy and sell, not only amongst themselves, but even with us.

(1636–1638), New England colonists fought the Pequot people for control of the valuable farmland and trading routes along the Connecticut River.

explanationText.text: England sometimes tried to eliminate other countries' control of trade by going to war with them.

content.text: passing laws to keep traders from the Netherlands out of English colonial ports

explanationText.text: Keeping traders from other countries away from North American ports was one way that the English controlled trade. Laws like these were meant to let English traders make money. Trade laws were also meant to give England an economic advantage over other countries, such as the Netherlands.

header.text: These choices are not correct:

content.text: passing laws to punish thieves in London, the English capital

explanationText.text: Laws such as these had to do with punishing criminals back in England. They would not have helped control trade in North America.

content.text: forbidding English people from going to North America

explanationText.text: English people in North America were needed in order to help England control trade and gain wealth and territory.

header.text: These choices are correct:

content.text: passing laws to keep traders from the Netherlands out of English colonial ports

explanationText.text: Keeping traders from other countries away from North American ports was one way that the English controlled trade. Laws like these were meant to let English traders make money. Trade laws were also meant to give England an economic advantage over other countries, such as the Netherlands.

content.text: going to war with countries who threatened English control of trade with North America

explanationText.text: England sometimes tried to eliminate other countries' control of trade by going to war with them.

header.text: These choices are not correct:

content.text: forbidding English people from going to North America

explanationText.text: English people in North America were needed in order to help England control trade and gain wealth and territory.

content.text: passing laws to punish thieves in London, the English capital

explanationText.text: Laws such as these had to do with punishing criminals back in England. They would not have helped control trade in North America.

The climate and growing conditions of the Middle Colonies allowed certain kinds of crops to grow well in the region. Early settlers to the Middle Colonies grew just enough food to survive. But over time, colonists began to grow enough food and other crops that they could sell some of what they grew. As a result, the economy of the Middle Colonies was largely based around growing
, or crops meant to be sold in other places.

content.text: Indentured servants often received land after their contracts ended.

elements.text: After a number of years, an indentured servant would usually be given some land in North America to farm. Land was expensive in Europe. For many poor Europeans, indentured servitude was the best chance of owning a farm.

elements.text: Traveling from Europe to North America was expensive. Poor Europeans could not afford the trip on their own.

header.text: The text below describes how historians use sources. Read the text. Then answer the question below.

elements.text: As historians examine each source, they ask what details it supports. If a certain detail is included in many different accounts, it is more likely to be true.

Historians ask who created the source and why. They also ask how the source was used at the time. They ask if the source was made for a specific audience. By asking these questions, historians can better determine which details in a source are more likely to be true.

elements.text: As historians examine each source, they ask what details it supports. If a certain detail is included in many different accounts, it is more likely to be true.

Historians ask who created the source and why. They also ask how the source was used at the time. They ask if the source was made for a specific audience. By asking these questions, historians can better determine which details in a source are more likely to be true.
